when: You are actively trying to falsify
text: {"foundGenuineWeakness":true,"weaknessDescription":"Three real weaknesses, none of which reverses the direction of the evidence. (1) Temporal mismatch: the release reports end-2014 data (Forbes March 2014, Credit Suisse 2014) and only PROJECTS the 1% share for 2016, so it does not directly measure the year the claim names. A defender of the claim could say 2016 is simply not observed here. (2) Modelled inputs: the bottom-half and top-1% shares come from a modelled global distribution that imputes wealth for data-poor countries and counts negative net worth (debt), so households in rich countries with mortgages or student loans can land in the 'poorest' groups. Both features distort the shares at the bottom, and the release concedes its counts shift with methodology (85 became 90 on re-estimation). (3) The publisher is a campaigning organisation that chose the comparison. However, the refuting inference does not depend on precision at the bottom. If roughly 48 million adults (the top 1%) hold about half of global wealth, then 80 individuals cannot hold 80% of it. That would require them to hold more than the entire top 1% does, and it is off by roughly two orders of magnitude from the release's own figure ($1.9 trillion for the richest 80, under 1% of a total in the hundreds of trillions). The weaknesses reduce confidence in the exact counts, not in the refutation."}

text: {"foundGenuineWeakness":true,"weaknessDescription":"The '62' figure was later disowned by its own author: Oxfam's January 2017 release says that with better India/China data the same comparison would have produced 9, not 62. So the specific count this source asserts for the year the claim names is wrong by a factor of about seven, and the source's bottom-half wealth estimate was materially too high. The negative-net-worth issue (indebted rich-country households counted as 'poor') also remains, despite the disclosed robustness check on the 1% share. Against the claim, though, the error runs the wrong way to help it. The revision makes the bottom half poorer, so it lowers the number of rich people needed to match it. It does not raise the share of global wealth those people hold. The richest 62's stated $1.76 trillion stays a small fraction of a global total in the hundreds of trillions, and the 1% share of about 50% caps what any few dozen individuals could hold far below 80%."}

Its date also cuts against using it as a 2026 statement either way: it describes March 2016 Forbes data, which is precisely why the claim's '8 in 2026' looks like a misdated version of it. None of this rescues the claim. The eight named fortunes sum to about $426 billion, a fraction of one percent of global household wealth, so the source cannot be read as eight people owning 80% of anything global."}

text: {"foundGenuineWeakness":true,"weaknessDescription":"The fact-check is not independent of the thing it checks in the way that matters: it re-derives Oxfam's figure from the same two inputs Oxfam used (the Credit Suisse databook and the Forbes list) rather than from a separate wealth-distribution estimate. Corroboration from Allianz and BCG covers only total financial wealth, not the bottom-half share. So any systematic error in Credit Suisse's modelling of the bottom of the distribution passes through both untouched. Its experts also flag that the databook may underestimate wealth in low-income countries, and that net worth is a poor poverty proxy. Those weaknesses bear on the bottom-half comparison, though, not on the scale needed here. Its anchor figures, total personal wealth of about $263 trillion and the richest 80 near $1.7 to 1.9 trillion, put the richest 80 at under 1% of the total. Even large errors at the bottom of the distribution cannot move that toward 80%."}
